one: In South Dakota, ask for your ballot by Monday, November 2, 2026.In South Dakota, the last day to ask for a mail ballot was Monday, November 2, 2026: you can still vote in person, early or on Election Day.In South Dakota, the last day to ask for a mail ballot was Monday, November 2, 2026: you can still vote in person on Election Day.
sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in South Dakota, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Monday, November 2Passed

You can apply in person at your county auditor's office during office hours or until 5 p.m. on Monday, November 2, 2026 (the day before the election), whichever is later. State law says no official may mail an absentee ballot after that Monday, so a request sent by mail now may not get a ballot back to you in time. (official page)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must reach your county election official on Election Day in time to be taken to your polling place before the polls close (polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., Tuesday, November 3, 2026). A ballot that arrives after the polls close is not counted. (official page)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

South Dakota’s own page on voting by mail

At school away from home, in South Dakota or in another state? What South Dakota says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. State law says any registered voter who is not otherwise disqualified may vote by absentee ballot. (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • By mail. Download the absentee ballot application, fill it in, sign it, and mail the signed original to your county election official (the county auditor). Either have your signature notarized on the application, or include a copy of your photo ID. Only military and overseas voters may send the application by fax or email. Open it (the law)
  • In person. Go to your county auditor's office during absentee voting, bring a photo ID, and vote there. If you have no photo ID, you can sign a personal identification affidavit instead and vote a regular ballot. (official page)
  • By a messenger. If you are confined by sickness or disability, you can apply in writing and have an authorized messenger bring the ballot to you and take it back. That request must reach the county election official before 3 p.m. on Election Day. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it in the return envelope to your county election official, early enough that it arrives before Election Day's deadline. (the law)
  • In person. Deliver it yourself to the county election official's office. (the law)
  • By a messenger. Give it to an absentee ballot messenger, who delivers it in person. A person who is a messenger for more than one voter must tell the election official every voter they are carrying for. (the law)

What the envelope needs

The application must be signed and either notarized or sent with a copy of your photo ID. The ballot itself needs no witness: mark it in private, seal it in the return envelope, and sign the statement on the envelope. Military and overseas voters do not need a notary or ID copy. (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on South Dakota’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Friday, September 18, 2026 to Monday, November 2, 2026.

In-person absentee voting at your county auditor's office began Friday, September 18, 2026 (state law sets it at 46 days before the election) and runs through Monday, November 2, 2026, during office hours (the Secretary of State says until 5 p.m. on the day before the election if that is later). Bring a photo ID, or sign an affidavit if you have none. (official page)

Students

At school in South Dakota, away from home

The Secretary of State says a South Dakota resident who moved to a new county for college has two choices: register where you live now (on campus or off campus), or stay registered and vote at your earlier home address in South Dakota. If you stay registered at home, you can ask that county for an absentee ballot. State law says a ballot is sent to your registration address or to a temporary address you give in writing. (official page)

At school in another state, with South Dakota as home

The Secretary of State's student page speaks to students from other states, not to South Dakotans at school elsewhere. State law says a South Dakota resident stays a resident while away if they intend to come back, and stays a resident of their county when they go to another state for a temporary purpose; they stop being a resident if they move meaning to become a resident of the other state. A student who keeps South Dakota as home can request an absentee ballot and give a temporary address where it should be sent. (official page)

Military and overseas

Military members, their families and U.S. citizens living overseas can ask for a ballot by mail, fax or email (the FPCA works too), with no notary or ID copy needed; those with a South Dakota driver's license can use the state's online portal. You can get the ballot by email, but you must print it and mail it back; marked ballots cannot be sent by fax or email. The application deadline is 5 p.m. the day before the election and the ballot must reach the county auditor before the polls close. If your ballot does not come, you can use the Federal Write-in Absentee Ballot for federal races. (official page)

South Dakota in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Since July 1, 2025, state law says a resident is someone who keeps a fixed home where they live and usually sleep for at least 30 days in a row. Since January 1, 2026, someone who registers or asks for an absentee ballot using only a mail-forwarding service or post office box as their home, without describing where they actually live, can vote only in federal races.
  • If you asked for an absentee ballot but are home on Election Day and have not voted it, the Secretary of State's military page says a registered voter may vote at their polling place; ask your county auditor how this works for you.
  • We did not find any statement on the state's pages about drop boxes, so none is described.
  • Poll hours (7 a.m. to 7 p.m.) come from the Secretary of State's College Students page (source 6).
  • That no official may mail an absentee ballot after the Monday before Election Day is in state law 12-19-5 (source 9).

How this was checked

  • The FVAP page loads by script and could not be read; it is linked, not quoted.

  • rest of the state: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. CST

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
